crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Client intake and triage in legal operations covers the structured capture of a prospective client's matter details, conflict checks, matter classification, urgency scoring, and routing to the right practice team or resource. It sits at the boundary between business development, risk management, and matter lifecycle management, and increasingly includes automated review of intake forms, email, and documents to extract parties, dates, jurisdictions, and legal issues. The goal is to reduce manual data entry, speed up conflict clearance, and ensure that high-risk or high-value matters are identified early.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the firm's existing intake stack: web forms, CRM, document management, email, and practice management or case management systems, with AI components typically deployed as APIs or embedded features inside those platforms. Because intake data includes confidential and often privileged prospective client information, the infrastructure must support role-based access, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logging, and data residency controls. Many firms run these tools in private cloud or on-premises environments rather than public multi-tenant services, and they rely on connectors to conflict databases and billing systems.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is a pipeline of document and text classification, named entity recognition, and rules-based or learned routing models. Intake forms and attachments are parsed to extract entities such as parties, courts, dates, and matter type, then compared against conflict databases using normalized names and fuzzy matching. Triage models assign a priority or complexity score based on factors like jurisdiction, opposing party, dollar amount, and practice area, and route the matter to an intake coordinator or attorney queue. Human review remains the final step for conflict clearance and engagement decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Client intake and triage raise direct duties around confidentiality, conflicts of interest, and unauthorized practice of law, so the output of any AI system must be treated as a recommendation, not a determination. Firms need written policies on data retention, model access, and human oversight, and they must ensure that automated conflict screening does not create a false negative that leads to a missed conflict. Because intake data often crosses state or national borders, privacy and data protection obligations apply, and the system should log every automated decision for audit and bar complaint defense.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Intake and triage tools are moving from simple form parsing toward conversational intake, where a prospective client describes a matter in natural language and the system asks follow-up questions to fill gaps. Future systems will likely integrate more deeply with court dockets, sanctions lists, and adverse party histories to flag risk before a conflict check is run. As firms adopt these tools, the bottleneck will shift from data entry to governance: proving that the triage logic is explainable, auditable, and consistent with the firm's ethical duties.
